16386.title: Cognitive Map
16386.heading: Cognitive Map
16386.content:
A cognitive map is the mental, hierarchical structure that represents the [[Spatial Knowledge]] a person obtains from an environment. It is stored in [[Long-Term Memory]] and used to understand position, orientation, routes, and relationships among places.

Cognitive mapping is the process of building, accessing, and using this structure. During [[Navigation]], perception and the cognitive map form a feedback loop: new environmental information updates spatial knowledge, while existing knowledge guides movement and interpretation.

Interfaces can support this process with stable landmarks, legible environments, maps, and transitions that preserve spatial context.

AR guidance can reduce immediate navigation effort by overlaying a route, yet it should still help the user relate the path to surrounding structure. Overview views, visible decision points, and [[Transitional Interface|transitions]] between perspectives preserve opportunities to build survey and route knowledge.

16389.title: Cognitive Load
16389.heading: Cognitive Load
16389.content:
Cognitive load is the amount of mental work required by a task or situation. It is shaped by external task demands, such as difficulty and priority, and by internal limits in [[Attention]] and [[Information Processing]]. Skills and well-formed mental structures can reduce the effort needed.

An interface raises cognitive load when users must remember transient information, divide attention, interpret unclear mappings, or control a secondary task such as [[3D Travel]] while performing a primary task.

Evaluation can combine subjective workload ratings with task-performance or physiological measures. Self-report is useful but is stronger when correlated with objective evidence.

In games, [[Articulatory Distance]] adds effort between intention and input, while [[Semantic Distance]] adds effort between feedback and understanding. These demands consume a finite [[Interactivity Budget]], so simultaneous fast action and complex reflection can overwhelm a player even when each demand is manageable alone.

16392.title: Cognition
16392.heading: Cognition
16392.content:
Cognition is the collection of processes that generate and use knowledge. It governs memory, language, and thought and is closely connected to [[Perception]] and [[Attention]].

Perceived stimuli are interpreted using representations and stored knowledge so that a person can reason, choose an action, and perform a task. In a [[3D User Interface]], cognition is especially important for complex tasks such as [[Wayfinding]], where the user must maintain [[Situation Awareness]], consult a [[Cognitive Map]], and make decisions while moving.

Interfaces can fail cognitively when they demand more attention or [[Working Memory]] than the user can supply.

16395.title: Cognitive Interactivity
16395.heading: Cognitive Interactivity
16395.content:
Cognitive interactivity consists of deliberate reasoning about tactics, strategy, planning, prediction, learning, and mastery. Short-term cognitive loops guide immediate choices, while long-term loops organize plans and progression.

It depends on understandable goals, sufficiently predictable consequences, and [[Systemic Depth]]. If the game supplies neither useful uncertainty nor a coherent model to learn, the player has little reason to think through its decisions.

16398.title: Cogeneration Power Plant
16398.heading: Cogeneration Power Plant
16398.content: A cogeneration plant supplies electricity and useful process heat from one fuel and conversion system. Steam can be extracted from a turbine at a suitable pressure, or gas-turbine exhaust and diesel-engine exhaust or cooling water can serve the heat demand. The source emphasizes industries and buildings needing both products at once. Total useful-energy efficiency rises when recovered heat displaces separate heat production.

16401.heading: Cofinal Ideal Filtrations
16401.content:
Two decreasing chains of ideals are cofinal when every term of either chain contains some term of the other. They eventually probe the same neighborhoods even if their indices differ.

Cofinal powers produce the same direct-limit local cohomology. In particular, replacing an ideal by another with the same radical does not change the resulting [[Local Cohomology]] modules.

16404.title: Coefficient Plot
16404.heading: Coefficient Plot
16404.content:
A coefficient plot displays regression estimates as points with uncertainty intervals around a no-association reference line. It makes the direction, magnitude, and precision of many adjusted effects easier to compare than a long output table.

Variables from the same conceptual domain can share a color, while labels replace terse code names. The plot assists interpretation but does not replace the numerical model table, which remains necessary for exact estimates and confidence intervals.

16407.title: Coefficient Matrix
16407.heading: Coefficient Matrix
16407.content:
The coefficient matrix of a [[Linear System]] contains the multipliers of the unknown variables. In $Ax=b$, it is the matrix $A$.

Its size, rank, sparsity, conditioning, and special structure determine which solving methods are appropriate. Appending the right-hand side forms the [[Augmented Matrix]].

16410.title: Code-First Development
16410.heading: Code-First Development
16410.content:
Code-first development defines persistent structure through application entity classes and mapping rules, then creates or updates the database from that model. It keeps the data model close to the source code and supports incremental schema evolution.

With [[Entity Framework Core]], a [[Database Context]] assembles the model and an [[Entity Framework Migration]] records the operations needed to bring the database schema into agreement with it.

The web-research project describes EF Core 3 as effectively code-first: application classes and configuration are the continuing source for the database model. An existing database can seed that process through reverse engineering, but later schema evolution proceeds from code.

16413.title: Cochain Complex
16413.heading: Cochain Complex
16413.content:
A cochain complex is a sequence C⁰ → C¹ → C² → ··· whose consecutive maps compose to zero. Its indices increase in the direction of the maps, unlike a [[Chain Complex]].

The quotient of cocycles by coboundaries gives a [[Cohomology Group]]. Injective resolutions and local cohomology are naturally expressed through cochain complexes.

16415.sourceSearchName: cobweb concept hierarchy cobweb concept hierarchy
16415.title: COBWEB Concept Hierarchy
16415.heading: Document

16416.sourceSearchName: cobweb concept hierarchy cobweb concept hierarchy
16416.title: COBWEB Concept Hierarchy
16416.heading: COBWEB Concept Hierarchy
16416.content:
A COBWEB concept hierarchy is a tree in which each node represents a probabilistic concept and terminal nodes can describe individual instances. Nodes store concept occurrence and attribute-value probabilities.

Adding an instance can update the stored statistics or restructure a local subtree through incorporation, new-disjunct, merge, or split operations. Skewed input can produce an unbalanced and expensive tree.

16417.sourceSearchName: cobweb concept hierarchy cobweb concept hierarchy
16417.title: COBWEB Concept Hierarchy
16417.heading: References

16419.title: COBWEB Clustering
16419.heading: COBWEB Clustering
16419.content:
COBWEB is an incremental conceptual-clustering algorithm that organizes nominal instances into a probabilistic hierarchy. Each concept node stores its occurrence probability and conditional probabilities for observed attribute values.

When a new instance arrives, the algorithm navigates the tree and selects a local operation using category utility. The structure is designed to improve inference about missing or unknown attributes.

16422.title: COBOL Portability
16422.heading: COBOL Portability
16422.content:
COBOL was designed as a common language for business data processing with readable, English-like statements. United States government procurement rules encouraged manufacturers to support it across otherwise incompatible computers.

The language achieved an early form of program portability when nearly the same program ran on machines from different vendors. Readable words did not eliminate the complexity of maintaining large programs over time.

16425.title: Coarticulation
16425.heading: Coarticulation
16425.content:
Coarticulation is the overlap of articulatory movements for neighboring speech sounds. A sound therefore changes acoustically depending on what comes before and after it.

This context dependence makes [[Continuous Speech Recognition]] harder than matching isolated word templates. An [[Acoustic Model]] must learn how phonetic realizations vary within real sequences.

16427.title: Coal Gasification for Hydrogen

16428.sourceSearchName: coal gasification for hydrogen coal gasification for hydrogen
16428.title: Coal Gasification for Hydrogen
16428.heading: Coal Gasification for Hydrogen
16428.content: Coal or heavy oil can undergo partial oxidation at high temperature to form a gas mixture from which hydrogen is recovered. The source describes converting accompanying carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide in catalytic stages, then scrubbing out CO2. This route produces hydrogen from a carbon-containing primary fuel and has different cost and energy yield from [[Steam Methane Reforming]] or [[Water Electrolysis]].

16431.title: Coaching Stance
16431.heading: Coaching Stance
16431.content:
A coaching stance combines neutrality, attention to the client's agenda, principle-guided action, and compassion. The coach listens for what the team is trying to achieve and helps it examine choices without covertly imposing a preferred answer.

Neutrality does not require indifference to harmful behavior or Scrum principles. It separates respect for the people from curiosity about the system and its results.

16434.title: Co-Training
16434.heading: Co-Training
16434.content:
Co-training uses two sufficiently informative views of each observation. A classifier trained on one view assigns confident pseudo-labels that enlarge the labeled set available to the classifier using the other view, and the exchange repeats.

The method relies on complementary views whose errors are not identical. If both views share the same bias or confident predictions are wrong, reciprocal pseudo-labeling can reinforce mistakes rather than add independent evidence.

16437.title: Co-Scheduling
16437.heading: Co-Scheduling
16437.content:
Co-scheduling runs several parallel applications at the same time and divides processors among them. A useful assignment exploits differing [[Application Speedup Profile|speedup profiles]] so the applications share capacity without unnecessarily extending the group's completion time.

For big-data workloads, alternating compute and I/O phases can create opportunities for one application to use resources another is not currently stressing.

16439.sourceSearchName: co located collaboration co located collaboration
16439.title: Co-Located Collaboration
16439.heading: Document

16440.sourceSearchName: co located collaboration co located collaboration
16440.title: Co-Located Collaboration
16440.heading: Co-Located Collaboration
16440.content:
Co-located collaboration occurs when participants share the same physical environment while working with related augmented content. Face-to-face speech, gesture, body orientation, and physical objects remain available alongside the digital channel.

The AR system should preserve these natural cues rather than isolating each person behind a private interface. Tracking and shared coordinates allow virtual objects to occupy the common workspace consistently for all participants.

16443.sourceSearchName: cnn rnn image captioning cnn rnn image captioning
16443.title: CNN-RNN Image Captioning
16443.heading: CNN-RNN Image Captioning
16443.content:
An image-captioning model can combine a [[Convolutional Neural Network]] encoder with a recurrent language decoder. The CNN analyzes the image and produces a vector representation; the recurrent component uses that vector as context while generating a description word by word.

Kelleher presents this as an intermodal variant of an [[Encoder-Decoder Network]]: the input is visual, but the output is a language sequence. The useful abstraction is not that a fixed vector perfectly captures an image's meaning; it is that learned representations can connect two different data forms in one trainable architecture.

16444.title: CNN-RNN Image Captioning

16445.title: CNN Receptive Field
16445.heading: Document

16446.sourceSearchName: cnn receptive field cnn receptive field
16446.title: CNN Receptive Field
16446.heading: CNN Receptive Field
16446.content:
A receptive field is the limited region of an input image inspected by one neuron in a [[Convolutional Neural Network]]. Early convolutional neurons take values from small neighboring pixel patches rather than the whole image. Neurons that share a detector can be placed at different positions, so their receptive fields collectively search for the same local feature across the image.

Neighboring fields may overlap. Their separation is controlled by [[Convolutional Stride]]. Later layers can combine responses from multiple local fields into features with broader spatial scope. The field is therefore an architectural choice about which input relationships a neuron can use directly.

16447.sourceSearchName: cnn receptive field cnn receptive field
16447.title: CNN Receptive Field
16447.heading: References

16448.sourceSearchName: cnn pooling layer cnn pooling layer
16448.title: CNN Pooling Layer
16448.heading: Document

16449.sourceSearchName: cnn pooling layer cnn pooling layer
16449.title: CNN Pooling Layer
16449.heading: CNN Pooling Layer
16449.content:
A pooling layer downsamples a [[Convolutional Feature Map]] by applying the same summary operation to successive local regions. Max pooling keeps the largest response in a region; average pooling keeps its mean. This reduces the amount of positional detail carried to the next stage.

Pooling can help a [[Convolutional Neural Network]] recognize a feature without depending on its exact location. The tradeoff is that detailed spatial relationships may be lost. Kelleher uses this limitation to motivate later models that aim to preserve how object parts are arranged, rather than treating the mere presence of parts as sufficient.

16450.sourceSearchName: cnn pooling layer cnn pooling layer
16450.title: CNN Pooling Layer
16450.heading: References

16451.sourceSearchName: cnn filter bank cnn filter bank
16451.title: CNN Filter Bank
16451.heading: Document

16452.sourceSearchName: cnn filter bank cnn filter bank
16452.title: CNN Filter Bank
16452.heading: CNN Filter Bank
16452.content:
One [[Convolutional Kernel]] detects one kind of local pattern. A convolutional network therefore trains multiple kernels, or filters, in parallel when it needs to detect different visual features. Each filter produces its own [[Convolutional Feature Map]], and the maps can be assembled into a multifilter representation.

A later convolutional layer may analyze that combined representation, or a [[CNN Dense Layer Integration|dense layer]] may combine all filter outputs to make a final decision. The bank expands what the network can represent without abandoning [[Convolutional Weight Sharing]] within each individual filter.

16453.sourceSearchName: cnn filter bank cnn filter bank
16453.title: CNN Filter Bank
16453.heading: References

16454.sourceSearchName: cnn dense layer integration cnn dense layer integration
16454.title: CNN Dense Layer Integration
16454.heading: Document

16455.sourceSearchName: cnn dense layer integration cnn dense layer integration
16455.title: CNN Dense Layer Integration
16455.heading: CNN Dense Layer Integration
16455.content:
A dense layer near the end of a [[Convolutional Neural Network]] can connect each of its neurons to all outputs from earlier filters. Unlike the shared weights within a convolutional filter, each dense neuron learns its own weights for combining those inputs.

This stage lets different neurons integrate the [[CNN Filter Bank|filter bank's]] local detections in different ways, such as relating simpler visual patterns to a whole-object decision. It is not another convolution: the dense connections collect information across the filter outputs rather than repeatedly applying one kernel to neighboring patches.

16456.sourceSearchName: cnn dense layer integration cnn dense layer integration
16456.title: CNN Dense Layer Integration
16456.heading: References

16457.title: CN2 Rule Induction
16457.heading: Document

16458.sourceSearchName: cn2 rule induction cn2 rule induction
16458.title: CN2 Rule Induction
16458.heading: CN2 Rule Induction
16458.content:
CN2 rule induction searches for a condition that covers a relatively pure subset of the training data, adds the resulting rule to an ordered list, and removes or downweights covered examples before continuing.

Its separate-and-conquer strategy builds one local rule at a time instead of recursively partitioning the whole space like a decision tree. Search control is needed because conjunctions of feature tests create many candidate antecedents.

16461.title: CMS Routing
16461.heading: CMS Routing
16461.content:
CMS routing maps a public URL, often built from an editor-controlled slug, to a stored content item and the template that renders it. In an ASP.NET Core system this mapping participates in the application's wider routing pipeline.

Slugs should remain unique within their intended scope and stable enough to serve as public identifiers. Changes need redirect or migration policies so editorial reorganization does not silently break incoming links.

A CMS page template converts structured content into a delivered page. It chooses the layout and renders the fields, regions, and components defined by the page's content type.

Keeping templates separate from stored content lets a site change presentation without rewriting every content item. Templates must nevertheless honor the content contract and handle optional or missing values predictably.

CMS media management stores and organizes assets such as images and documents so editors can reuse them in content. The system tracks metadata, media types, and storage locations while exposing assets through its editing and delivery APIs.

Media is both content and a security boundary. Upload rules, file types, sizes, naming, access controls, and generated variants should be managed deliberately rather than treating arbitrary files as harmless page decoration.

A CMS content type defines the structured shape and editorial purpose of an item. Sites, pages, and posts can have different fields, behaviors, and templates even when they share the same publishing system.

Explicit types turn editorial expectations into a model that software can validate and render. A useful type is broad enough for recurring content but narrow enough that its fields have stable meaning across every instance.

A CMS authenticates editors before granting access to management functions and authorizes what each identity may view or change. Publishing, administration, media management, and ordinary editing can require different permissions.

Editorial access should be separated from public content delivery and follow least privilege. The surrounding application's identity and authorization mechanisms remain responsible for enforcing these boundaries consistently across pages and APIs.

16482.title: Clutching
16482.heading: Clutching
16482.content:
Clutching occurs when a manipulation cannot be completed in one motion, forcing the user to release, reposition, and reengage the control before continuing.

A wrench used in a confined space is a physical example. In a [[3D User Interface]], limited device range or an unsuitable control mapping can produce the same repeated interruption during [[Object Positioning]] or [[Object Rotation]].

Clutching is wasted motion that can reduce performance and comfort. A precision grip, motion amplification, or a mapping with a more suitable range can reduce the number of regrasping cycles, though amplification can also reduce fine control.

16485.content:
A CluStream microcluster is a compact statistical summary of nearby stream observations. It records sufficient information such as counts, linear and squared sums, and temporal statistics so that centroids, radii, and time properties can be recovered without storing every point.

Online processing updates or creates microclusters, while an offline phase groups snapshots into larger clusters for a chosen time horizon. The separation lets users analyze historical periods after the raw stream has passed.

Wrappers can capture interactions among features and the biases of the chosen algorithm, but repeated clustering makes them expensive. They can also overfit an internal quality measure, so stability and external domain interpretation remain necessary.

16491.heading: Clustering-Based Outlier Detection
16491.content:
Clustering-based outlier detection treats observations in very small or sparse clusters, or outside all normal clusters, as anomaly candidates. A hierarchical approach can cut a dendrogram and inspect the smallest groups.

The result depends on the cut level, distance, and clustering method. Normal points can form small clusters, while outliers can be absorbed when the grouping is too coarse.

16494.heading: Clusterwise Redshift Regression
16494.content:
The book uses astronomical redshift measurements to illustrate precision-based search. Photometric redshift is easier to obtain but less precise than spectrometric redshift, so the project groups measurement pairs by shared decimal prefixes before considering local matching or regression.

The cluster is defined by similarity in the measured redshift values, not by sky location. A prefix tree can retrieve candidate pairs rapidly from a large survey, but any regression still needs its own accuracy assessment: shared digits identify a useful search neighborhood, not a guaranteed physical relationship.

The Template Method pattern places the invariant sequence of an algorithm in a base-class operation and delegates selected steps to overridable hooks. ClusLib's public clustering operation coordinates argument setup, computation, result reset, and result transfer.

Derived algorithms reuse the lifecycle while implementing their distinctive calculation. Protected hooks prevent clients from invoking a partial sequence, and pure virtual hooks make missing behavior a compile-time error.

A clustering solution space contains candidate partitions produced by varying algorithms, parameters, initializations, features, or constraints. Exploring that space treats clustering as selection among defensible organizations rather than generation of one unquestioned answer.

Distances or transitions among solutions help an analyst locate stable regions and meaningful alternatives. The display must summarize a very large space without implying that nearby solutions are equally useful for the application.

The pattern is appropriate only when uniqueness is a real invariant. Its global lifetime and hidden dependency can complicate testing, so clustering components should not become singletons merely for convenient access.

16506.content:
A clustering level function records the proximity value at which each stage of a hierarchy is formed. It gives the vertical scale of a dendrogram and assigns a cophenetic proximity to every pair of observations.

Large jumps between adjacent levels can suggest a useful stopping point because the next merge joins groups that were substantially farther apart under the chosen linkage.

16509.heading: Clustering Filter Feature Selection
16509.content:
A filter method ranks or selects features before the final clustering algorithm is run. It uses properties of the data such as variance, redundancy, local geometry, or spectral consistency rather than feedback from a particular clusterer.

Filters are usually computationally efficient and reusable across algorithms. Their independence is also a limitation because a feature score can preserve generic structure without improving the specific grouping objective used downstream.

Keeping the catch at the application boundary avoids repeated handling inside every numerical routine. Internal functions should throw when invariants fail and allow the boundary to decide how the complete operation terminates.

The abstraction should contain only genuinely common responsibilities. Moving every possible option into the base class produces coupling, whereas focused extension points allow new algorithms, distances, adapters, or visitors to enter the framework independently.

16518.heading: Clustering Hybrid Feature Selection
16518.content:
A hybrid feature-selection method combines a fast filter with a clustering-aware refinement. The filter narrows the candidate set, and a wrapper or embedded stage then tests how the surviving features affect cluster structure.

This design reduces the search cost of a pure wrapper while retaining more task sensitivity than a standalone filter. Its result depends on both stages, so the filtering threshold must not discard dimensions that become useful only in combination.

16521.title: Clustering Feature Microcluster
16521.heading: Clustering Feature Microcluster
16521.content:
A clustering feature summarizes a set of numeric points by its count, coordinate-wise linear sum, and squared sum. These quantities are additive, so summaries from disjoint groups can be merged without revisiting their members.

Centroids, radii, and within-group dispersion can be derived from the tuple. The summary is efficient but cannot reconstruct arbitrary shapes or distributions, so compression is most faithful for compact local groups.

16524.title: Clustering Argument Validation
16524.heading: Clustering Argument Validation
16524.content:
Clustering argument validation turns algorithm assumptions into executable preconditions. A cluster count must be positive and no greater than the record count, seeds must be valid, iteration limits must be positive, and input data must have the required attribute types.

Checking before allocation or iteration yields clearer failures and protects later calculations from impossible state. Error messages should identify both the parameter and its allowed domain.

16527.title: Clustering Categorical Data
16527.heading: Clustering Categorical Data
16527.content:
Categorical data clustering groups records whose attribute values have no inherent numeric order. Ordinary geometric distance cannot be applied directly to values such as sunny, red, or regulatory.

Algorithms therefore define similarity through matching values, co-occurrence, shared neighbors, graph connectivity, or supported projections. The representation should respect attribute cardinality and meaning.

16530.title: Clustering Analysis
16530.heading: Clustering Analysis
16530.content:
Clustering analysis divides observations into groups so members of the same group are more similar to one another than to members of other groups. It is unsupervised because no supplied class label defines the desired partition.

Results depend on the similarity measure, representation, algorithm, parameters, and assumed cluster shape; a partition is not meaningful independently of those choices.

The introductory treatment in *Cluster Analysis and Data Mining* frames clustering as a sequence of explicit choices: select attributes, define proximity, form groups whose within-group similarities exceed between-group similarities, choose a stopping level, and validate the interpretation. A clustering is therefore conditional on its representation, objective, parameters, and intended use.

16532.sourceSearchName: clustering algorithm lifecycle clustering algorithm lifecycle
16532.title: Clustering Algorithm Lifecycle
16532.heading: Document

16533.sourceSearchName: clustering algorithm lifecycle clustering algorithm lifecycle
16533.title: Clustering Algorithm Lifecycle
16533.heading: Clustering Algorithm Lifecycle
16533.content:
The ClusLib lifecycle runs argument setup, the concrete clustering computation, result reset, and result fetching in a fixed public sequence. Clients invoke clusterize rather than calling protected stages themselves.

The ordering validates configuration before numerical work and clears the prior public result before transferring the newly computed one. Derived classes can vary individual hooks while preserving a complete execution.

16534.sourceSearchName: clustering algorithm lifecycle clustering algorithm lifecycle
16534.title: Clustering Algorithm Lifecycle
16534.heading: References

16536.title: Cluster Validity
16536.heading: Cluster Validity
16536.content:
Cluster validity is the assessment of whether a clustering accurately represents meaningful structure. It asks whether within-cluster relationships, between-cluster separation, and the selected number of groups are supported by evidence.

Validity can be evaluated against known labels, from the data and proximities alone, or by comparison with alternative solutions. The criteria must match the method and intended interpretation.

16539.title: Cluster
16539.heading: Cluster
16539.content:
A cluster is a group of observations that are similar to one another with respect to selected attributes and comparatively different from observations in other groups. In cluster analysis, neither the number of groups nor their defining characteristics must be supplied in advance.

A cluster is therefore defined operationally by the representation, the [[Proximity Measure]], and the grouping rule. Changing any of those choices can change which observations appear to belong together.

16541.sourceSearchName: cluster tree visitor pattern cluster tree visitor pattern
16541.title: Cluster Tree Visitor Pattern
16541.heading: Document

16542.sourceSearchName: cluster tree visitor pattern cluster tree visitor pattern
16542.title: Cluster Tree Visitor Pattern
16542.heading: Cluster Tree Visitor Pattern
16542.content:
The Visitor pattern moves operations on a node hierarchy into a separate class family. Each leaf or internal node accepts a NodeVisitor and dispatches to the overload matching its concrete node type.

ClusLib uses visitors to collect join values, build flat partitions, and draw dendrograms without embedding every operation in Node. Adding a new visitor is easy, while adding a new node type requires changing the visitor interface and each concrete visitor.

16543.sourceSearchName: cluster tree visitor pattern cluster tree visitor pattern
16543.title: Cluster Tree Visitor Pattern
16543.heading: References

16544.sourceSearchName: cluster tree composite pattern cluster tree composite pattern
16544.title: Cluster Tree Composite Pattern
16544.heading: Document

16545.sourceSearchName: cluster tree composite pattern cluster tree composite pattern
16545.title: Cluster Tree Composite Pattern
16545.heading: Cluster Tree Composite Pattern
16545.content:
The Composite pattern represents individual leaves and nested groups through one node interface. In a clustering tree, LeafNode stores a record and InternalNode stores child nodes, while both answer traversal and size operations through their common Node base.

Clients can treat a complete hierarchy and a single leaf uniformly, which simplifies partition extraction and rendering. Parent links, child ownership, levels, and join values must remain consistent as nodes are combined.

16546.sourceSearchName: cluster tree composite pattern cluster tree composite pattern
16546.title: Cluster Tree Composite Pattern
16546.heading: References

16548.title: Cluster Stability
16548.heading: Cluster Stability
16548.content:
Cluster stability is the degree to which a grouping persists after reasonable changes to the analysis. Cases can be added or removed, features perturbed, starting configurations varied, or samples regenerated and the resulting partitions compared.

A stable result is less likely to be an accident of one sample or initialization. Stability does not prove substantive meaning, but instability is an important warning.

16551.title: Cluster Separation
16551.heading: Cluster Separation
16551.content:
Cluster separation measures how distinct a cluster or observation is from competing clusters. For a point, it can be defined as the smallest average distance to the members of another cluster.

Strong separation complements cohesion. A grouping can contain internally compact clusters yet remain poor if those clusters are not distinguishable from each other.

16553.sourceSearchName: cluster seed point cluster seed point
16553.title: Cluster Seed Point
16553.heading: Document

16554.sourceSearchName: cluster seed point cluster seed point
16554.title: Cluster Seed Point
16554.heading: Cluster Seed Point
16554.content:
A cluster seed point is an initial representative used to begin a partitioning algorithm. Each observation can be assigned to its nearest seed before centroids are recomputed.

Useful seeds should cover the occupied regions of attribute space. Poorly placed or duplicate seeds can create unstable, empty, or locally suboptimal clusters.

16555.sourceSearchName: cluster seed point cluster seed point
16555.title: Cluster Seed Point
16555.heading: References

16556.sourceSearchName: cluster result interpretation cluster result interpretation
16556.title: Cluster Result Interpretation
16556.heading: Document

Tags: [[Cluster Data Quality and Interpretation]]

16557.sourceSearchName: cluster result interpretation cluster result interpretation
16557.title: Cluster Result Interpretation
16557.heading: Cluster Result Interpretation
16557.content:
Cluster result interpretation assigns substantive meaning to the groups, boundaries, and relationships produced by an algorithm. It examines characteristic attributes, within-group variation, separation, overlap, and exceptions.

Interpretability depends on the method: a K-means cluster is organized around a centroid, while a density cluster or probabilistic component has a different meaning. Validation evidence and domain knowledge must accompany the label.

16558.sourceSearchName: cluster result interpretation cluster result interpretation
16558.title: Cluster Result Interpretation
16558.heading: References

16560.title: Cluster Recovery
16560.heading: Cluster Recovery
16560.content:
Cluster recovery is the extent to which an algorithm reconstructs a known or simulated grouping from observed data. Recovery studies vary sample size, cluster count, dimensionality, separation, noise, and method, then compare captured and true partitions.

An external validity index quantifies the match. Strong recovery under controlled conditions reveals capability but does not guarantee performance on an unknown real-world structure.

16563.title: Cluster Reassignment
16563.heading: Cluster Reassignment
16563.content:
Cluster reassignment moves an observation from its current group to another when the alternative representative provides a better fit under the objective function. Centroids may then be updated to reflect the changed memberships.

Repeated reassignment drives iterative partition methods toward convergence. The final solution is locally stable under the permitted move, not necessarily globally optimal.

16565.sourceSearchName: cluster prototype cloning cluster prototype cloning
16565.title: Cluster Prototype Cloning
16565.heading: Document

16566.sourceSearchName: cluster prototype cloning cluster prototype cloning
16566.title: Cluster Prototype Cloning
16566.heading: Cluster Prototype Cloning
16566.content:
The Prototype pattern creates an object by cloning an existing representative rather than selecting its concrete class explicitly. A virtual clone operation delegates copying to the runtime type, preserving derived schema or component behavior.

Cloning is useful when algorithms manipulate polymorphic objects through base pointers. The design must specify whether referenced data are copied deeply or shared, because an unintended shallow copy can couple centers, schemas, or prototypes that should evolve independently.

16567.sourceSearchName: cluster prototype cloning cluster prototype cloning
16567.title: Cluster Prototype Cloning
16567.heading: References

16568.sourceSearchName: cluster membership vector representation cluster membership vector representation
16568.title: Cluster Membership Vector Representation
16568.heading: Document

16569.sourceSearchName: cluster membership vector representation cluster membership vector representation
16569.title: Cluster Membership Vector Representation
16569.heading: Cluster Membership Vector Representation
16569.content:
A cluster membership vector stores, at position i, the index of the cluster assigned to record i. It is a compact representation for hard partitions and is used as the common result field across ClusLib algorithms.

The vector assumes a stable record order and cluster-index convention. Fuzzy memberships, hierarchy, centers, or diagnostics require additional structures because one integer per record cannot express them.

16570.sourceSearchName: cluster membership vector representation cluster membership vector representation
16570.title: Cluster Membership Vector Representation
16570.heading: References

16572.title: Cluster Projection
16572.heading: Cluster Projection
16572.content:
A cluster projection is the subset of values from one attribute that participates in a categorical cluster. CACTUS first finds projections relative to other attributes, intersects them, and then synthesizes projections across the full attribute set.

Projection lets the method build a multidimensional categorical cluster from supported lower-dimensional relationships.

16575.title: Cluster Homogeneity
16575.heading: Cluster Homogeneity
16575.content:
Cluster homogeneity is the degree to which observations within the same cluster resemble one another. High within-cluster similarity is one side of a useful grouping; the other is strong [[Between-Cluster Separation]].

Homogeneity is always relative to the attributes and proximity measure used. A group can be homogeneous for one purpose while concealing important differences for another.

16577.sourceSearchName: cluster feature vector cluster feature vector
16577.title: Cluster Feature Vector
16577.heading: Document

16578.sourceSearchName: cluster feature vector cluster feature vector
16578.title: Cluster Feature Vector
16578.heading: Cluster Feature Vector
16578.content:
A cluster feature vector is a compact triple containing the number of points, their linear sum, and their squared sum. These sufficient summaries can be combined by addition and support centroid, radius, and dispersion calculations without retaining every original point at each tree node.

BIRCH uses the vector to summarize subclusters while scanning a large data set.

16579.sourceSearchName: cluster feature vector cluster feature vector
16579.title: Cluster Feature Vector
16579.heading: References

16580.sourceSearchName: cluster feature tree cluster feature tree
16580.title: Cluster Feature Tree
16580.heading: Document

16581.sourceSearchName: cluster feature tree cluster feature tree
16581.title: Cluster Feature Tree
16581.heading: Cluster Feature Tree
16581.content:
A cluster feature tree is a height-balanced hierarchy that stores [[Cluster Feature Vector|cluster feature vectors]]. Internal entries point to child summaries, while leaf entries represent bounded-diameter subclusters and are connected for later global clustering.

Branching and diameter thresholds control memory and compression. Inserting a point updates ancestor summaries and may split nodes or increase the tree height.

16582.sourceSearchName: cluster feature tree cluster feature tree
16582.title: Cluster Feature Tree
16582.heading: References

16583.sourceSearchName: cluster analysis objective function cluster analysis objective function
16583.title: Cluster Analysis Objective Function
16583.heading: Document

16584.sourceSearchName: cluster analysis objective function cluster analysis objective function
16584.title: Cluster Analysis Objective Function
16584.heading: Cluster Analysis Objective Function
16584.content:
A cluster analysis objective function assigns a numerical quality to a proposed grouping. An algorithm searches for merges, splits, or reallocations that improve this value, such as reducing within-cluster squared error or limiting loss of information.

The objective defines what the algorithm regards as a good cluster. Because distinct objectives reward different shapes and balances, optimizing one perfectly does not establish that its solution is uniquely correct for the application.

16585.sourceSearchName: cluster analysis objective function cluster analysis objective function
16585.title: Cluster Analysis Objective Function
16585.heading: References

16586.sourceSearchName: cluster ensemble problem cluster ensemble problem
16586.title: Cluster Ensemble Problem
16586.heading: Document

16587.sourceSearchName: cluster ensemble problem cluster ensemble problem
16587.title: Cluster Ensemble Problem
16587.heading: Cluster Ensemble Problem
16587.content:
The cluster ensemble problem combines several partitions of the same observations into one consensus without assuming that cluster labels correspond across inputs. Labels are arbitrary, so direct voting by label name is invalid.

Consensus methods instead use co-membership, graph, probabilistic, or relabeling structures. Their goal is to recover stable shared evidence while reducing sensitivity to individual algorithms, samples, or initializations.

16588.sourceSearchName: cluster ensemble problem cluster ensemble problem
16588.title: Cluster Ensemble Problem
16588.heading: References

16590.sourceSearchName: cluster density variation cluster density variation
16590.title: Cluster Density Variation
16590.heading: Cluster Density Variation
16590.content:
Cluster density variation occurs when some groups occupy compact, crowded regions while others are sparse or diffuse. One global distance threshold or centroid objective can split a sparse cluster or absorb an outlier near a dense cluster.

Local-density methods and sensitivity analysis help address the problem. The reported result should explain how unequal densities affected parameter and algorithm choice.

16591.sourceSearchName: cluster density variation cluster density variation
16591.title: Cluster Density Variation
16591.heading: References

16593.title: Cluster Cohesion
16593.heading: Cluster Cohesion
16593.content:
Cluster cohesion measures how closely related the observations within one cluster are. A common point-level definition uses the average distance from an observation to the other members of its assigned group.

Low within-cluster distance indicates strong cohesion under the selected metric. It is combined with [[Cluster Separation]] in the silhouette measure.

16595.sourceSearchName: cluster co association matrix cluster co association matrix
16595.title: Cluster Co-Association Matrix
16595.heading: Document

16596.sourceSearchName: cluster co association matrix cluster co association matrix
16596.title: Cluster Co-Association Matrix
16596.heading: Cluster Co-Association Matrix
16596.content:
A cluster co-association matrix records how often each pair of observations appears in the same cluster across an ensemble. It converts label-invariant partition evidence into a similarity matrix.

A standard clusterer can partition the matrix to obtain consensus groups. The representation captures pairwise agreement but loses higher-order structure, and a homogeneous ensemble may make shared bias look like strong evidence.

16597.sourceSearchName: cluster co association matrix cluster co association matrix
16597.title: Cluster Co-Association Matrix
16597.heading: References

16599.title: Cluster Centroid
16599.heading: Cluster Centroid
16599.content:
A cluster centroid is the component-wise mean of the observations assigned to a numerical cluster. It serves as the center used by K-means and related methods for distance comparisons.

A centroid summarizes location but not spread, density, or shape, and it need not be an observed data point. Outliers and attribute scale can move it substantially.

16601.sourceSearchName: cluster analysis workflow cluster analysis workflow
16601.title: Cluster Analysis Workflow
16601.heading: Document

16602.sourceSearchName: cluster analysis workflow cluster analysis workflow
16602.title: Cluster Analysis Workflow
16602.heading: Cluster Analysis Workflow
16602.content:
A basic cluster analysis workflow represents observations through attributes, computes similarities or dissimilarities, applies a grouping algorithm, selects a stopping level or number of groups, and interprets and validates the result.

Each stage can change the outcome. Attribute selection, scaling, the [[Proximity Measure]], initialization, stopping rules, and treatment of outliers should therefore be documented as part of the result rather than hidden as preprocessing details.

16603.sourceSearchName: cluster analysis workflow cluster analysis workflow
16603.title: Cluster Analysis Workflow

16605.title: ClusLib Schema Class
16605.heading: ClusLib Schema Class
16605.content:
Schema is a container of shared AttrInfo objects plus metadata for labels and identifiers. It sets those special values on records, tests schema compatibility, and provides virtual comparison behavior for derived schema types.

Because every record refers to the same schema, type interpretation stays consistent across a dataset. Its virtual destructor and clone behavior support polymorphic use without losing a derived schema's structure.

16608.title: ClusLib Results Object
16608.heading: ClusLib Results Object
16608.content:
Results contains the hard cluster membership vector and inherits a map for named algorithm-specific outputs. Its reset operation clears both the common vector and the additional result values before a fresh result is published.

Clients receive a const reference so they can inspect but not rewrite the algorithm's answer. Centers, hierarchies, errors, likelihoods, iterations, or fuzzy matrices can be returned under explicit keys.

16611.content:

Container methods provide indexed value access, while record methods expose identity and optional class information. Copying a record can share its immutable schema rather than duplicating the entire attribute-description graph.

Keeping headers and source files for one subject together makes the design topology visible in the filesystem. Separate example directories give each algorithm an executable client without mixing demonstration code into reusable components.

16632.title: ClusLib Dataset Class
16632.heading: ClusLib Dataset Class
16632.content:
Dataset inherits a container of shared Record pointers and owns a shared Schema pointer. Construction requires a schema, and the class exposes record counts, attribute counts, typed cell access, numeric or categorical checks, saving, and membership extraction.

The schema is returned through a const reference so its meaning cannot be casually replaced after dataset construction. Copy and assignment behavior must keep record and schema ownership consistent.

16635.title: ClusLib Cluster Container
16635.heading: ClusLib Cluster Container
16635.content:
The ClusLib Cluster base class is a typed container of shared Record pointers with a cluster identifier. It captures the property common to one-center, multi-center, fuzzy, and subspace concepts: each cluster denotes a collection of records.

A virtual destructor supports derived cluster types, while inherited container methods handle membership access and modification. Algorithm-specific summaries can be added by subclassing without duplicating record storage behavior.

16638.title: ClusLib Arguments Object
16638.heading: ClusLib Arguments Object
16638.content:
Arguments packages the shared inputs common to clustering algorithms: a dataset pointer, an optional distance pointer, and named values inherited from Additional. Clients obtain a mutable reference and configure the algorithm before starting its public lifecycle.

Keeping the object inside Algorithm gives every method one parameter channel while allowing concrete classes to define extra names. Each implementation must retrieve and validate the entries it requires.
